p.seg: Without the worthies one lacks the means to face urgencies,
and without the scholares one has no one with whom to consider matters of state.
For anyone to be slow in showing respect to the worthies, to overlook the scholars
or to be capable to cause his state to be preserved intact:
such a thing has never occurred.
In ancient times “Duke” （he was only a marquis and had only the honorific posthumous title of a "Duke") Wen fled into exile in order to put the world aright.
"Duke" Huan of Qi left his state to become the hegemon of (all) the Feudal Lords.
King Gou Jian of Yue had encountered the wicked acts from the part of the King Wu
and went on to dominate the worthy rulers of the the central states:
the reason why these three people were capable of making a name for themselves and achieving a substantial impact on the oikoumene (world)
was that within their states they were suppressed and suffered ugly maltreatment.
The best case is never to suffer any defeat (in the first place).,
the next best is, when defeated to have what it takes to bring things to a successful end:
this is what is meant by "the proper use of the people".
I am told:
Thus the true gentleman finds himself more difficult than everything else.
In making progress the true gentleman does not defeat his (high) aspirations.
At home he tries to get to the bottom of the inner reality of his feelings,
and even being mixed together with ordinary folks
right to the end he harbours no resentment (against the authorities):
That man is the sort of person believes in himself.
Thus he who works for what he finds difficult
is bound to get what he desires in this；
I have never heard of anyone working for what he desires
and (thereby) escaping what he hates.
Therefore pushy powerful ministers are harmful to the ruler
and sycophantic subjects are harmful to their superiors.
A ruler should always have thoughtfully dissenting ministers
and any superior should always have subordinates ready to make objections.
